title: Reduce long-context tail latency by eliminating scheduler queue starvation
creator: Lina Chen
description:
Summary:
Several customers across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private environments have escalated severe 95/99th token-latency regressions over the last month. Root cause traces point to the continuous-batching scheduler entering a starvation state when a small number of very long-context requests monopolize batch assembly and kernel scheduling. This ticket coordinates a set of short-term bugfixes and a longer-term scheduler resilience plan to prevent queue starvation and reduce long-context tail latency.

Incidents observed:
- Multiple Hosted customers reported sudden spike in chat turn latencies (95p > 2s for short replies) coinciding with background long-context vectorization jobs.
- One Dedicated customer saw production stalls during nightly bulk inference with mixed request shapes; autoscaler kept nodes healthy but tail latency for low-latency endpoints spiked.
- Two Private deployments reproduced queue backlog locally when KV-cache eviction and very long prompts caused the batching window to stretch > 200ms and starve small requests.

Impact:
- Customer-facing P99 increases, user-visible timeouts, and support escalations.
- Workloads that rely on sub-200ms responses (search snippets, UI autocomplete) are intermittently degraded.

Root cause hypothesis (combined):
1) The continuous-batching scheduler groups requests by availability and kernel-fit; long-context requests push batch formation thresholds higher (max sequence length dominates token budget), increasing wait time for short requests.
2) Priority/preemption path is disabled in several backends when KV-cache warmup is running, creating head-of-line contention.
3) Eviction-triggered cache churn causes additional scheduling stalls as model KVs are reloaded, amplifying backlog.
4) Adaptive floodgate heuristics fail for multi-tenant mixes (e.g., one tenant doing few very large requests plus many small ephemeral requests).

Reproduction steps (engineers):
1) Canary environment: replay a mix of 5% long-context (>=32k tokens), 65% medium (4–8k tokens), 30% short (<512 tokens) requests at steady QPS.
2) Enable KV-cache replication toggles to reproduce eviction interaction.
3) Observe batch-formation histograms, per-route wait-time, and kernel scheduling logs.
4) Confirm that small requests experience median wait time > batch-formation target and increased P95/P99 generation latency.

Short-term mitigations (goal: rollback customer impact within 48–72 hours):
- Fix #1: Enforce batch-window upper bound (configurable per-route). If batch window would exceed X ms (initially 50ms), flush and process partial batches to avoid long waits for small requests.
- Fix #2: Route-aware priority tokens: classify routes as latency-sensitive vs throughput-first; prefer forming small low-latency batches when tokens available.
- Fix #3: Re-enable preemption path during KV-cache warmup (bug: warmup currently disables preemptive queues). Patch to keep preemption active.
- Fix #4: Backpressure/signaling: when a single request would cause excessive per-batch token budget (>Y tokens), surface 429 or 413 to the client in shared-hosted pools or route into dedicated/long-request pools.

Long-term changes (follow-up epics):
- Scheduler rewrite to a token-aware fairness queue (lease-based scheduling) that enforces per-tenant and per-route fairness without head-of-line blocking.
- KV-cache eviction smoothing: stagger eviction and background reloads to avoid synchronized stalls.
- Enhanced perf tests in the continuous integration harness that simulate mixed-shape tenants and measure tail latency regressions.

Acceptance criteria:
- Canary results: For a mixed workload described above, small-request P95 latency must return to within 10% of baseline and P99 below our SLO for the route.
- No regressions on throughput-heavy benchmarks (>99% of baseline for median tokens/sec).
- New unit/integration tests added and green in CI.
- Customer validation: 2 impacted customers confirm improvements on Hosted/Dedicated pilots.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge short-term fixes behind feature flag and deploy to canary pool (runtime-1.22-canary).
2) Monitor Grafana dashboards, alert on any increase in median latency or error rate for affected routes.
3) Progressive rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% of Hosted traffic over 24–48 hours if canary metrics are stable. Dedicated customers get opt-in pilot; Private customers receive patch bundles and a scheduled upgrade window.
4) If any regression observed, rollback flag per cluster; emergency rollback runbook in Confluence link.

Testing and observability additions:
- New histograms: per-request "batch_wait_ms" annotated by request_length_bucket and route.
- Export events when preemption is used and when batch window is forced to flush early.
- Add chaos test that injects KV eviction and long-request spike during steady short-request QPS.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How aggressive should the "max batch window" be by default for global Hosted customers vs Dedicated? (Tuning required).
- Trade-off between cost (more partial batches -> higher GPU inefficiency) and latency guarantees; aim to provide per-customer knobs.

Notes / Related:
- This ticket is intentionally conservative: short-term changes prioritize correctness and safety with feature flags. Long-term scheduler work will be broader but tracked separately under runtime-scheduler-epic.
